params.text:
Fire extinguishers and the PASS technique

Extinguishers are for tackling a very small fire only — and only if it is safe to do so, you have a clear escape route behind you, and you have raised the alarm first. Your safety and the residents' safety always come first: if there is any doubt, get out and let the fire service deal with it. Using the wrong type of extinguisher can make a fire far worse, so it is vital to know what each colour is for. In the UK, extinguisher bodies are red with a coloured label or band showing the type.

If you ever need to use an extinguisher on a small fire, remember PASS:

  • P – Pull the safety pin.
  • A – Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, not the flames.
  • S – Squeeze the handle to release the extinguishing agent.
  • S – Sweep from side to side across the base of the fire.

Always keep an escape route behind you and back away if the fire does not go out quickly.

Fire classes and choosing the right extinguisher

Fires are grouped into classes by what is burning, and using the wrong extinguisher can make matters far worse. You are not expected to be an expert, but a basic awareness helps you understand the equipment around you and why it is placed where it is. Colour-coded labels help you tell the types apart.

  • Class A — solids such as paper, wood and fabric: water or foam.
  • Class B — flammable liquids such as petrol or spirits: foam, carbon dioxide or powder.
  • Class C — flammable gases: the supply should be shut off; powder may be used.
  • Class F — cooking oils and deep fat: wet chemical extinguishers.
  • Electrical fires: carbon dioxide (CO2) suits live electrical equipment and leaves no residue.

Dry powder is versatile but creates a choking cloud that is unpleasant and hard to see through indoors. Fighting a fire is always a last resort. Only ever tackle a small fire if you have been trained, it is not spreading, you have raised the alarm first, and you have a clear escape route at your back. Never use water on electrical equipment or on a cooking-oil fire. If you are in any doubt at all, get out and leave it to the fire service.

params.question: A small fire has started in live electrical equipment. Which extinguisher is most suitable, and what is the safest overall approach?

answers.text: Carbon dioxide (CO2), but only tackle it if trained, it is not spreading and you have raised the alarm and kept an escape route.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. CO2 suits electrical fires, and fighting any fire is a last resort that depends on training, a contained fire and a clear exit.

answers.text: A water extinguisher, aimed straight at the equipment.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Water conducts electricity and must never be used on live electrical equipment; CO2 is the safer choice.
Incorrect. Wet chemical is designed for cooking-oil (Class F) fires, not electrical equipment.

answers.text: Any extinguisher will do, so grab the nearest one and start spraying.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Using the wrong extinguisher can make a fire worse, and fighting a fire is only ever a last resort when it is safe to do so.
